summary: Specifies how the MPLS DetNet data plane and encapsulation work over an IP network, based on the existing MPLS-over-UDP technique.

eli5.summary: MPLS-style packets get wrapped in ordinary UDP packets so they can cross plain IP networks.

questions: what is detnet mpls over udp
how does detnet work over ip networks
which udp source port does detnet use
subtitle: How DetNet's MPLS packets ride inside ordinary UDP/IP packets across an IP network.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking flows need a sequence number, OAM marking and flow identification, but an IP network has no MPLS labels to carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The DetNet MPLS encapsulation is kept (control word, S-Label, optional F-Labels), and UDP and IP headers replace or follow the F-Labels, following the MPLS-in-UDP method of RFC 7510.
tldr.outcome: DetNet MPLS flows can cross an IP network and are then handled as DetNet IP packets, within a single administrative control or a closed group of them.

facts.label: IP versions
facts.value: IPv4, IPv6 and IPv6 Segment Routing

facts.label: UDP source port
facts.value: MUST uniquely identify the DetNet flow

today: RFC 9025 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2021. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why MPLS DetNet Over IP
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) offers flows extremely low packet loss and an assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. Background is in RFC 8655.

To carry DetNet MPLS flows with full functionality over an IP network, four things are required: a way to identify DetNet flows, a way to carry the DetNet sequence number, a way to tell DetNet OAM packets from data packets, and a way to carry queuing and forwarding indication. The MPLS encapsulation of RFC 8964 provides all of them. The DetNet IP data plane of RFC 8939 only partly does, because it carries no DetNet sequence number.

This document therefore maps the MPLS encapsulation onto the DetNet IP data plane, modeled on MPLS over UDP from RFC 7510.
sections.eli5: The special packages need tracking labels that plain mail does not carry. So the labels are kept, and the whole package goes inside a normal envelope.

sections.title: Where It May Be Used
sections.content:
RFC 7510 says that MPLS-in-UDP MUST NOT be used over the general Internet, or over non-cooperating network operators, to carry traffic that is not congestion controlled.

The RFC states that this constraint does apply to DetNet, because DetNet is constrained to operate within a single administrative control or within a closed group of administrative control.
sections.eli5: These special packages only travel on roads owned by one company or a small club of friendly companies, not on the whole public highway.

sections.title: The UDP/IP Encapsulation
sections.content:
The design may partly or entirely replace the F-Labels of RFC 8964 with UDP and IP headers. The UDP and IP header information is used to identify DetNet flows, including member flows. There may be zero or more F-Labels between the S-Label and the UDP header.

From the top, a packet carries the DetNet app-flow payload, the DetNet control word, the S-Label, optional F-Labels, the UDP header and the IP header. The first group is the DetNet data plane MPLS encapsulation, and the UDP and IP headers are the DetNet data plane IP encapsulation.

S-Labels, A-Labels (when present), the d-CW and any F-Labels are used as defined in RFC 8964 and are not modified. The encapsulation works equally well with IPv4, IPv6 and IPv6-based Segment Routing (RFC 8754).
sections.eli5: The package keeps its own labels inside. The outer envelope has an address that the normal mail system understands.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Procedures
sections.content:
To send, an implementation MUST support provisioning of UDP and IP header information in addition to or in place of F-Labels. When packet replication is done at the MPLS service sub-layer there are several member flows, and each one needs its own UDP and IP header information.

The headers MUST be formatted according to the configuration and as defined in RFC 7510, and the UDP Source Port value MUST be set to uniquely identify the DetNet flow. The packet MUST then be handled as a DetNet IP packet per RFC 8939, including QoS-related traffic treatment.

To receive, an implementation MUST support provisioning of received UDP and IP header information. That information MUST be used to identify incoming app flows from the combination of S-Label and incoming encapsulation header information. Normal receive processing from RFC 8964, including the Packet Elimination Function (PEF) and Packet Ordering Function (POF), can then take place.
sections.eli5: The sender writes a different return address on the envelope for each flow. The receiver looks at the envelope and the inner label together to know which flow a package belongs to.

sections.title: What Must Be Configured
sections.content:
The minimum configuration for DetNet MPLS over UDP/IP is: label information (A-Labels, S-Labels and F-Labels) mapped to UDP/IP flows, the IPv4 or IPv6 source and destination addresses, the DSCP field (in the IPv4 Type of Service or IPv6 Traffic Class), the UDP source port, the UDP destination port, and whether the UDP checksum is used. A single S-Label can map to several sets of UDP/IP information when packet replication, elimination and ordering (PREOF) is used.

This information MUST be provisioned per DetNet flow, for example by the controller or the management plane. Not using the UDP checksum has to be evaluated case by case, using the exception criteria in RFC 7510, particularly with IPv6.

The DetNet Controller Plane is responsible for provisioning both flow identification information and the resources that give each flow the treatment it needs. With network or port address translation in the path, the Controller Plane decides what information is needed for correct mapping at sender and receiver.
sections.eli5: Someone in charge has to write down, for every flow, which addresses and numbers go on the envelope, and make sure the roads have room for it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The solution reuses mechanisms from other documents, so their security considerations apply equally. The RFC singles out RFC 7510, since this is mainly an application of MPLS-over-UDP, and also points to DetNet security in general, RFC 8655, and the MPLS and IP considerations in RFC 8964 and RFC 8939. It adds no security considerations of its own.

It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: It adds no new safety rules. The rules of the pieces it reuses still apply.
